chapters.title: Reconciliation
chapters.subtitle: Turning enemies into friends, face to face
chapters.trueMeaning: enmity changed into friendship and peace
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew Bible has no single word for "reconcile". Instead it tells stories of faces turned toward each other again, gifts that soften anger, people who return and make peace. The Greek word Paul uses means changing enemies into friends, and in the New Testament it is always God who does the reconciling, reaching out to us and to the whole world.
chapters.bigIdea: Reconciliation is broken relationships made whole again: God takes the first step toward us, and we are sent to take that step toward each other.
skeleton: In English, "reconcile" means to bring two sides back together after a quarrel.
Hebrew has no single word for it; it uses pictures: covering a face, being accepted, returning, making peace.
Jacob and Esau, and Joseph and his brothers, show what reconciliation looks like in real families.
Jewish teaching says God's forgiveness on Yom Kippur does not cover wrongs against a neighbour until the neighbour is appeased.
Jesus says the same: go and be reconciled to your brother first, then bring your gift.
Paul's Greek word katallassō means changing enemies into friends, and God is always the one who reconciles.
God reconciles people to Himself, people to each other, and in the end "all things".
Those who are reconciled are given a ministry of reconciliation.

p: In everyday English, to **reconcile** means to bring two people back together after a quarrel, or to make two sets of numbers agree. In church we often hear that Jesus "reconciled us to God", but the picture can be vague. Many people imagine an angry God who had to be calmed down before He would accept us.

The Bible's own words paint a richer and warmer picture. Hebrew has no single word that matches "reconcile". Instead it uses several vivid pictures: covering an angry face, being accepted with pleasure, turning back home, and making peace. Greek, the language of the New Testament, has a family of words that mean **changing enmity into friendship**. Looking at both helps us see what reconciliation really is.

sections.h: Hebrew pictures: a face, a welcome, a return
p: The first picture comes from Jacob. Afraid of meeting his brother Esau, he sends gifts ahead and says, "I will appease him with the present" (Genesis 32:20; 32:21 in Hebrew). The Hebrew literally says *akhapperah panav*, "I will cover his face". The verb is *kipper*, the same word used for atonement. Here it means calming someone's anger so that the two can look at each other again.

A second word is *ratsah*, "to be pleased with, to accept". In Leviticus 1:4 an offering "shall be accepted for him", meaning the worshipper is welcomed by God. A third is *shuv*, "to turn back, return". God calls, "Return to me, and I will return to you" (Malachi 3:7). Reconciliation is a two-way turning.

A fourth picture is simply **making peace**. In Isaiah 27:5 God invites even His enemies: "Let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me." The phrase is *asah shalom*, to make shalom. Shalom is more than the end of fighting; it is wholeness, things put right between people.

The Torah shows reconciliation in two great family stories. Jacob had cheated Esau and fled for twenty years. When they finally meet, Esau runs to him, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, and they weep (Genesis 33:4). Jacob then says, "To see your face is like seeing the face of God, and you have accepted me" (33:10). "Accepted" is *ratsah* again. The night before, he had wrestled with God and said he had seen God face to face (32:30).

Joseph's brothers sold him as a slave. Years later, as ruler in Egypt, he reveals himself, weeps aloud, and kisses them (Genesis 45). Later he tells them, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (50:20), and he comforts them and speaks kindly to them.
> In both stories reconciliation is costly and physical: tears, embraces, gifts, honest words. It is the healing of a real relationship, not a legal adjustment on paper.

sections.h: Greek words: changing enemies into friends
p: The main Greek words are *katallassō*, "to reconcile", and the noun *katallagē*, "reconciliation". They come from a verb meaning "to change" or "to exchange". Lexicons note that the word could be used of exchanging money, but its common meaning was changing hostility into friendship between people, for example a wife and husband (1 Corinthians 7:11).

Paul uses a stronger form, *apokatallassō*, in Ephesians and Colossians: Christ reconciles Jews and Gentiles "both to God in one body through the cross", killing the hostility (Ephesians 2:16), and God was pleased "to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:20).

Jesus himself, in Matthew 5:24, uses yet another word, *diallassomai*: "first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift." It appears only here in the New Testament. It is the ordinary word for two people settling a quarrel, and Jesus puts it right next to the altar: peace with your brother comes before your offering to God.

Here is a striking detail. In some Jewish Greek writings before the New Testament, God is described as the one who "is reconciled" to His people after His anger (for example 2 Maccabees 7:33). Paul turns this around. In the New Testament, **God is never the one who needs to be reconciled**. God is always the one who reconciles.

"While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). "All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself" (2 Corinthians 5:18). "In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them" (5:19). The hostility that needed to change was on our side. God did not wait for us to calm Him down; He came to us, like Esau running to meet Jacob.

Jewish tradition is very practical here. The Mishnah teaches: "For sins between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones. For sins between a person and his neighbour, the Day of Atonement does not atone until he has appeased his neighbour" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). The verb for "appease" there is the same *ratsah* we met in Leviticus.

For this reason, Jews traditionally go to people they have hurt in the days before Yom Kippur and ask forgiveness. Later Hebrew calls this *piyyus*, "appeasing". Jewish tradition teaches that if the person refuses, you should try again, more than once, and that the injured person should not be cruel and refuse forever.

Jesus teaches the same thing in Matthew 5:23–24: if you are at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift, go, be reconciled, and then come back. Reconciliation with people is not an optional extra to worship. It is part of it.

In the Torah, someone who wronged another person had to confess and also **make restitution**: pay back in full and add a fifth (Numbers 5:6–7). Saying sorry was not enough if something had been stolen or damaged. Reconciliation in the Bible is practical: the person who caused the harm works to repair it, so that trust can grow again.

This is exactly what Zacchaeus does when Jesus comes to his house. He says, "Half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Jesus answers, "Today salvation has come to this house." Reconciliation with God showed itself immediately in putting things right with people.

sections.h: Common misunderstandings and the Jewish lens
p: A common Western picture says that God was the offended party who had to be changed, and that reconciliation is mainly a legal transaction about our status before Him. The Bible's words point another way. The enmity was ours; God took the first step; and reconciliation is a restored relationship, like brothers embracing.

Another misunderstanding is that reconciliation is only "me and God". In Ephesians 2, the cross breaks down the wall between Jews and Gentiles and makes "one new humanity", and Christ "himself is our peace" (2:14). In Colossians 1:20 the scope is "all things". Reconciliation is personal, communal and cosmic.

Jacob's words in Genesis 32:20 show the problem. The Hebrew says "I will cover his face". The KJV gives "I will appease him" and the NIV "I will pacify him". Translators chose this because "cover his face" means nothing in English, and the sense really is calming Esau's anger. But the reader loses the link with *kipper*, the word behind "atonement", and the theme of the face that runs through the whole story. The Septuagint kept both: it uses *exilaskomai*, a Greek word it also uses for atonement, with "his face".

Older English shows how words shift. In Romans 5:11 the KJV says we "have now received the atonement", where the Greek is *katallagē*, reconciliation. In 1611 "atonement" still meant "at-one-ment", being made one again. The same Bible uses "reconciliation" for the Hebrew *kipper*, as in Daniel 9:24, "to make reconciliation for iniquity". Over time the two English words have drifted apart, and today "atonement" sounds mainly like paying a penalty. Modern versions say "reconciliation" in Romans 5:11 to keep the original sense.

A third loss is that one English word covers several originals. "Be reconciled" translates *diallassomai* in Matthew 5:24, *katallassō* in 2 Corinthians 5:20 and *apokatallassō* in Colossians 1:20, and it also stands for several Hebrew pictures. Translators keep one word because the ideas are close and readers need clarity. But the variety reminds us that reconciliation reaches all the way from a quarrel between brothers to the healing of the whole creation.

In Jacob's world a quarrel was never only between two people. It touched honour, family and property. The normal way to approach someone you had wronged, or someone more powerful, was with a gift and with bowing. Jacob's present is called a *minchah* (Genesis 32:13), the same word later used for the grain offering, and he bows to the ground seven times (Genesis 33:3), like a subject before a king. Then Esau surprises everyone: the injured brother runs, embraces and welcomes first.

Villages and clans in the Middle East have long had public ways of making peace: elders who mediate, a gift, a shared meal, and an embrace in front of others so that everyone knows the feud is over. The Bible's stories have the same public and physical shape. Joseph weeps so loudly that the Egyptians hear it (Genesis 45:2), and a family that was broken eats together again.

In the Greco-Roman world *katallassō* belonged to family life and to politics. It was used of a husband and wife coming back together, and of cities ending a war through envoys. Paul borrows that political picture: "we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us" (2 Corinthians 5:20). Usually it was the weaker or defeated side that sent envoys asking for terms. Here the stronger side, God himself, sends the envoys and pleads, "be reconciled".

Paul says God "gave us the ministry of reconciliation" and that we are "ambassadors for Christ… be reconciled to God" (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). People who have been welcomed home are sent to help others come home, and to make peace in their families, churches and towns.

In practice this looks like the old Jewish custom before Yom Kippur: going to the person you hurt, admitting the wrong, repairing what you can, and being ready to forgive when someone comes to you. It is rarely easy. But every time a face that was turned away turns back, we see a small picture of what God is doing in the whole world.

words.missed: English "appease" or "pacify" drops the picture of covering a face, and hides the link with kipper, the Bible's atonement word.
words.culture: In the ancient Near East you approached an offended or powerful person with a gift and low bows, as Jacob does with his present and his seven bows (Genesis 33:3).

words.note: Being welcomed with favour; the Mishnah uses it for appeasing a neighbour you wronged.
words.missed: "Accepted" sounds like a formal approval; ratsah is warmer: being looked on with pleasure and welcomed.
words.culture: At the Temple the question was whether an offering was "accepted"; in daily life it was the smile of a host or a king who receives you.

words.note: "Return to me, and I will return to you": reconciliation as a two-way turning.
words.missed: Versions switch between "return", "turn" and "repent", so readers miss that one verb describes both people and God turning.
words.culture: Exiles coming home, runaway sons and travellers on the road all "returned"; it is a word of roads and homecoming.

words.note: God invites even His enemies to make shalom with Him.
words.missed: "Make peace" can sound like signing a ceasefire; shalom also means wholeness, health and well-being for both sides.
words.culture: Shalom was the everyday greeting, so making shalom meant people could greet each other again.

words.note: Going to someone you hurt to ask forgiveness, especially before Yom Kippur.
words.missed: It is not a Bible word, so English Bibles never show it, and "apology" is too small for the effort it describes.
words.culture: Jewish custom is to visit the people you have hurt in the days before Yom Kippur and ask forgiveness face to face.

words.note: To change enmity into friendship; in the NT God is always the one who reconciles.
words.missed: "Reconcile" can sound like balancing accounts; the Greek is about enemies becoming friends.
words.culture: Greeks used it for an estranged husband and wife coming back together, and for cities ending a war.

words.note: The gift we receive and the ministry we are given.
words.missed: The KJV calls it "the atonement" in Romans 5:11, a word whose meaning has since narrowed to paying for sin.
words.culture: In public life it described the settling of a feud or a war; Paul makes it a gift that God gives.

words.note: A stronger form: Jews and Gentiles in one body, and "all things" reconciled.
words.missed: English has only "reconcile" again, so the extra force of "completely, back again" is lost.
words.culture: Paul writes for a world split between Jews and Gentiles, where a wall in the Temple kept Gentiles out of the inner courts.

words.note: Jesus: first be reconciled to your brother, then offer your gift.
words.missed: Bibles use the same "be reconciled" as for God's great work, so the everyday flavour of "settle it with your brother" is hidden.
words.culture: Jesus speaks to people who carried offerings to the Temple, often after a long journey, yet he tells them to leave the gift and go.

quiz.q: What does Jacob literally say he will do with his gift in Genesis 32:20?
options: Pay a fine to the priests
quiz.why: The Hebrew is akhapperah panav, "I will cover his face", using kipper to mean calming Esau's anger.

quiz.q: According to Mishnah Yoma 8:9, when does Yom Kippur atone for a wrong against a neighbour?
options: Only if a sacrifice is offered
Only after the neighbour has been appeased
quiz.why: Sins between people are not atoned for until the person who did wrong has appeased the one he hurt.

quiz.q: In the New Testament, who is the one who reconciles?
options: The angry party, who must be calmed
No one; it happens by itself
quiz.why: God reconciles us and the world to Himself (2 Corinthians 5:18–19); He is never described as the one who needs to be reconciled.

quiz.q: What did Zacchaeus do that showed true reconciliation?
options: He paid back those he cheated fourfold
quiz.why: Like the Torah's law of restitution, he repaired the damage he had caused (Luke 19:8).

quiz.q: How wide is the reconciliation described in Colossians 1:20?
options: All things, on earth or in heaven
quiz.why: God was pleased to reconcile to himself all things, making peace by the blood of the cross.

quiz.why: In 1611 "atonement" meant being made "at one"; modern versions translate katallagē as "reconciliation".

chapters.title: Confess and Confession
chapters.subtitle: Why the same word means "I have sinned" and "Thank You, God"
chapters.trueMeaning: agreeing with God's truth, and praising Him
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew, the word for confessing sin and the word for giving thanks and praise come from the same root. In Greek, "confess" literally means to say the same thing, to agree. Biblical confession is not grovelling: it is telling the truth about ourselves and about God, together with others, and it naturally turns into praise.
chapters.bigIdea: To confess is to agree with God out loud about the truth, about our sin and about His goodness, so that confession and praise belong together.
skeleton: We usually think of confession as a private, gloomy admission of wrongdoing.
In Hebrew, hitvaddah (confess) and hodah (give thanks, praise) come from the same root, yadah.
Todah can mean both a thank offering and a confession; Judah's name means "praise".
Jewish confession (viddui) is said aloud, often together, in the plural: "we have sinned".
The Greek homologeō means "to say the same thing": to agree, admit and declare.
Exomologeomai covers both confessing sins and praising God, just like the Hebrew.
Confession is made to God, and also to the people we have wronged.
Honest confession leads to healing, forgiveness and joy.

p: When many people hear the word **confession**, they picture something private and heavy: a whispered list of failures, a feeling of shame, maybe a booth in a church. Others think of a police confession, admitting guilt so the punishment can begin.

The Bible's words carry a surprise. In Hebrew, the word for confessing sin and the word for thanking and praising God come from **one and the same root**. In Greek, "confess" literally means "to say the same thing". Confession, in the biblical world, is about telling the truth and agreeing with God. And it does not end in shame. It ends in praise.

sections.h: One Hebrew root: confess and give thanks
p: The root is *yadah* (י־ד־ה). In one verb form, *hitvaddah*, it means "to confess": "he shall confess the sin he has committed" (Leviticus 5:5). On the Day of Atonement the high priest lays his hands on the goat and "confesses over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel" (Leviticus 16:21). After the exile, the people "stood and confessed their sins" (Nehemiah 9:2).

In another form, *hodah*, the same root means "to give thanks, to praise": *hodu ladonai ki tov*, "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good" (Psalm 136:1). Yet *hodah* can also mean confess: "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD" (Psalm 32:5), and "whoever confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy" (Proverbs 28:13).
> The root idea seems to be **openly acknowledging** something. You can acknowledge your sin, or you can acknowledge God's goodness. In the Bible, the two often happen in the same breath.

The noun *todah* usually means thanksgiving, or a thank offering (Leviticus 7:12). But when Joshua confronts Achan, who had stolen from the spoils, he says: "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give him *todah*" (Joshua 7:19). Here it means "make confession to him". Telling the truth about his sin was a way of giving God honour.

The same root gives us the name **Judah**. When Leah's fourth son was born she said, "This time I will praise the LORD" (*odeh*), and named him *Yehudah* (Genesis 29:35). Since the word "Jew" comes from Judah, the very name of the Jewish people is tied to this word for praise and acknowledgement.

The Hebrew noun for confession is *viddui*. Jewish confession is traditionally **spoken aloud**, and on Yom Kippur it is said together, in the plural. The *Ashamnu* runs through the Hebrew alphabet: "We have been guilty, we have betrayed, we have robbed…" The longer *Al Chet* repeats, "For the sin which we have sinned before You…" Many worshippers gently strike their chest at each line.

Everyone says "we", even for sins they personally did not commit. Jewish tradition teaches that the community stands together and carries responsibility together. The prophets prayed this way too. Daniel, a faithful man, prays, "We have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly" (Daniel 9:5), and Nehemiah and Ezra do the same.

The Mishnah describes the high priest on Yom Kippur confessing aloud, "I have done wrong, I have transgressed, I have sinned before You", first for himself and his house, then for the priests, then for all Israel (Mishnah Yoma 3:8; 4:2; 6:2). It also teaches that a condemned man should be urged to confess, "for everyone who confesses has a share in the world to come", learning this from Achan (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:2).

sections.h: Greek words: saying the same thing
p: The main Greek verb is *homologeō*. It is built from *homo-*, "same", and *logos*, "word": literally "to say the same thing". In use it means to agree, to admit, and to declare publicly. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9). To confess sin is to say about it what God says about it.

The same verb is used for openly declaring faith: "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9–10). The noun *homologia* means "the confession" of faith that believers hold together: "Let us hold fast our confession" (Hebrews 4:14).

Hebrews 13:15 joins the ideas beautifully: "Let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name." Here confessing is praising, just as in Hebrew. When we agree with God about who He is, that agreement naturally becomes worship.

A second verb, *exomologeomai*, means to confess or acknowledge openly. People came to John the Baptist "confessing their sins" (Matthew 3:6). James writes, "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed" (James 5:16).

Yet the same verb is used for praise. Jesus prays, "I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth" (Matthew 11:25), and Paul says "every tongue" will "confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:11). This is no accident. In the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint, *exomologeomai* is the usual word for *hodah*: "Give thanks to the Lord" in Psalm 136:1. The Greek carried the Hebrew double meaning straight into the New Testament.

sections.h: Confessing to God and to people
p: In the Torah, confession comes with action. Someone who wronged another person must confess and make restitution (Numbers 5:6–7). Jewish tradition teaches that confessing to God is not enough for wrongs against a neighbour; you must also go to the person (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). Jesus says the same in Matthew 5:23–24.

The returning son in Jesus' parable rehearses his confession: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you" (Luke 15:18). "Heaven" is a respectful Jewish way of saying "God". He confesses to both God and his father. James 5:16 shows that the early church kept this practice: confession among believers, with prayer, leading to healing.

Hebrew has one root, *yadah*, for confessing sin and for giving thanks. English has no word that does both, so translators must choose each time: "O give thanks unto the LORD" in Psalm 136:1, but "I will confess my transgressions" in Psalm 32:5, though the verb is the same. In Joshua 7:19 the KJV rightly says "make confession unto him" for a word that usually means a thank offering. These are good choices for clear reading, but the reader never sees that, in the Bible, admitting the truth and praising God are one movement.

Interestingly, the older chain of translations kept the link. The Septuagint used *exomologeomai* for both, and the Latin Vulgate used *confiteor* for both: "Confitemini Domino, quoniam bonus", "Confess to the Lord, for he is good". For centuries Latin readers heard confession and praise in the same word. English split them apart. The same happens in the New Testament: *exomologeomai* is "confessing" in Matthew 3:6 but "I thank thee" or "I praise you" in Matthew 11:25, and Hebrews 13:15 turns "lips confessing his name" into "giving thanks" (KJV).

Church history also coloured the word. In the medieval Western church, confession became part of the sacrament of penance, said privately to a priest, and later in a booth. That practice gave "confession" a private, guilty tone that the Hebrew *viddui* and the Greek *homologeō* do not have. And when the KJV says "our profession" in Hebrews 4:14, a modern reader may think of a job; the Greek *homologia* is the confession of faith believers say together.

In Israel, confession and thanksgiving both happened at the Temple, in public. A person bringing a sin offering confessed the wrong (Leviticus 5:5). A person rescued from danger brought a *todah*, a thank offering, and told the story before the congregation: "I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving… in the presence of all his people" (Psalm 116:17–18). The todah was then eaten as a meal with family and friends. Thanks was not a private feeling; it was a feast and a testimony.

This was an honour-and-shame culture, where losing face in public was a serious thing. That makes public confession costly. Achan confesses before all the tribes (Joshua 7:19–21), and Israel confesses together, "we have sinned". Yet the Bible turns the shame upside down: telling the truth "gives glory to God", and the one who confesses finds mercy (Proverbs 28:13).

In the Greco-Roman world *homologeō* was a word of contracts and courts. People used it for agreeing to terms, signing that a debt was owed, or admitting a charge before a judge. So "confessing" Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9) sounded like making a public, binding statement of loyalty. In an empire where loyal citizens said "Caesar is Lord", that confession could cost a great deal, as early Christian martyr stories show.

sections.h: Common misunderstandings and living it out
p: One misunderstanding is that confession is about making ourselves feel as bad as possible so that God will accept us. The Bible's words point the other way: confession is **agreement with the truth**, and God, who already knows, is "faithful and just to forgive". Another is that confession is purely private. The Bible shows it spoken aloud, often together, and to the people we have wronged.

David describes the relief: "When I kept silent, my bones wasted away… I said, 'I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,' and you forgave the iniquity of my sin" (Psalm 32:3–5). The psalm opens and closes with joy. Try it this week: name a wrong honestly to God, make it right with anyone involved, and then thank Him out loud. That is the full shape of biblical confession.

words.note: One root behind both confessing sin and giving thanks.
words.missed: English must choose "confess" or "thank" each time, so readers never see that one root lies behind both.
words.culture: Israelites acknowledged God aloud at the Temple, in song and in testimony before others, never only in private thought.

words.note: Confessing sin aloud, by a person, a priest, or the whole people.
words.missed: "Confess" today can sound like a private, guilty whisper; hitvaddah was spoken aloud, often over a sacrifice.
words.culture: A worshipper bringing a sin offering confessed the wrong (Leviticus 5:5); on Yom Kippur the high priest confessed over the goat for the whole people.

words.gloss: to give thanks, praise; also confess
words.note: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good"; the same verb is used for confessing sin.
words.missed: English splits it into "give thanks" (Psalm 136:1) and "confess" (Psalm 32:5), hiding that these are the same verb.
words.culture: Hodu ladonai ki tov was sung by Levites and crowds at Temple festivals and is still sung in the Jewish Hallel.

words.note: A thank offering, but Joshua uses it for Achan's confession.
words.missed: Translations rightly say "make confession" in Joshua 7:19, but the reader loses that the word normally means a thank offering.
words.culture: The todah offering was eaten as a joyful meal with family and friends, after a vow was paid or a rescue celebrated.

words.note: Leah says "I will praise the LORD"; the word "Jew" comes from this name.
words.missed: "Judah" and "Jew" look like plain names in English; the link with praise is invisible.
words.culture: Names in Israel often recorded a parent's prayer or praise at the birth, as Leah's naming shows.

words.note: Confession said aloud, together, in the plural: Ashamnu and Al Chet.
words.missed: The English "confession" brings to mind a church booth; viddui is a shared prayer said by the whole congregation.
words.culture: On Yom Kippur the Ashamnu and Al Chet are said standing, many gently striking the chest at each line.

words.note: Literally "to say the same thing": agreeing with God out loud.
words.missed: "Confess" hides the literal picture "say the same thing", agreeing with God's verdict.
words.culture: In Greek contracts and courts it meant to agree to terms, to acknowledge a debt or to admit a charge.

words.note: The Septuagint's usual word for hodah, so it carries both meanings.
words.missed: Bibles render it "confess" in one place and "thank" or "praise" in another, so its double meaning is lost.
words.culture: Through the Septuagint it was the word Greek-speaking Jews sang in the Psalms: "Give thanks to the Lord".

words.note: The shared confession of faith that believers hold fast.
words.missed: The KJV's "our profession" (Hebrews 4:14) sounds like a job; the Greek is the confession of faith we share.
words.culture: Early Christians had short spoken confessions such as "Jesus is Lord", in a world where loyal citizens said "Caesar is Lord".

rows.literal: acknowledge / thank the LORD, for he is good

The context demands "confess", so the usual meaning "thanksgiving" disappears, and with it the idea that truth-telling honours God.
Correct in context, but readers cannot see it is the verb used for "confessing their sins" in Matthew 3:6.

Mainly about feeling bad

verses.text: I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.
Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.
Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
We have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.

keyPoints: In Hebrew, hitvaddah (confess) and hodah (give thanks, praise) come from the same root, yadah: openly acknowledge.
Todah can mean a thank offering or a confession (Joshua 7:19); Judah's name means "I will praise".
Jewish confession (viddui) is spoken aloud and, on Yom Kippur, together in the plural: "we have sinned".
The Greek homologeō literally means "to say the same thing": to agree with God, admit and declare.
Exomologeomai means both confessing sins and praising God, because the Septuagint used it for hodah.
Confession includes going to the person we wronged and making restitution (Numbers 5:6–7; Matthew 5:23–24).
Honest confession leads to forgiveness, healing and joy (Psalm 32; 1 John 1:9; James 5:16).
reflect: Do you think of confession as heavy and shameful, or as telling the truth to a faithful God? What would change if you saw it as the start of praise?
Is there a wrong you need to confess not only to God but to a person?
How might praying "we have sinned" with others change the way you see your church or community?

quiz.q: What surprising link do the Hebrew words for "confess" and "give thanks" share?
options: They come from the same root, yadah
One is Greek and one is Hebrew
They are only used in Leviticus
quiz.why: Hitvaddah (confess) and hodah (give thanks, praise) both come from yadah, "openly acknowledge".

quiz.q: What does the Greek homologeō literally mean?
quiz.why: Homo- (same) + logos (word): to agree, to say about something what God says about it.

quiz.q: How is the Yom Kippur confession traditionally said?
options: Only by those who committed the sins
quiz.why: Ashamnu and Al Chet are said by the whole congregation: "we have sinned".

quiz.q: Which name comes from the same root as "confess" and "praise"?
quiz.why: Leah said "I will praise the LORD" and named him Yehudah (Genesis 29:35).

quiz.q: According to James 5:16, what follows when believers confess to one another and pray?
quiz.why: "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed."

quiz.q: Why do English Bibles say "give thanks" in Psalm 136:1 but "confess" in Psalm 32:5?
options: They are two unrelated Hebrew words
English has no single word for the Hebrew verb hodah, which covers both
The KJV made a copying mistake
quiz.why: Both verses use forms of yadah; the Latin Vulgate kept one word (confiteor), but English must choose.

chapters.title: Prayer
chapters.subtitle: The service of the heart, at set times and in every moment
chapters.trueMeaning: the heart's service, standing before God
chapters.nutshell: Hebrew has many words for prayer: interceding, entreating, asking, calling on God's name, pouring out the heart, pleading for grace and blessing. Jews prayed at set times, together, with words they shared, yet with the heart fully present. Jesus and his followers prayed the same way, and the Lord's Prayer sounds like the Jewish prayers around it.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical prayer is "service of the heart": a rhythm of shared, regular prayer and honest, personal pouring out of the heart before God.
skeleton: We often think of prayer as asking God for things, alone and in our own words.
Hebrew has a whole vocabulary of prayer: hitpallel, atar, sha'al, qara beshem, siach, techinnah, berakhah.
The rabbis called prayer "service of the heart" and stressed kavanah, focused intention.
Jews prayed at fixed times: morning, afternoon and evening, and recited the Shema twice a day.
The Greek proseuchomai, deēsis, aiteō, enteuxis and eucharisteō cover praying, petition, asking, intercession and thanks.
Jesus and the apostles kept the Jewish hours and forms of prayer.
The Lord's Prayer closely echoes Jewish prayers such as the Kaddish.
Prayer is both fixed and free, both "we" and "I".

p: For many Christians, **prayer** means talking to God in our own words, usually alone, and usually asking for something. Set prayers or written prayers can feel cold or "religious". Fixed times of prayer might seem like rules rather than relationship.

The Hebrew Bible and Jewish practice offer a much wider picture. There are many Hebrew words for prayer, each showing a different side of it. Jews prayed at regular hours, often together, with shared words, and yet they insisted that the heart must be in it. Jesus and the apostles grew up in exactly this world of prayer.

The most common Hebrew verb for "pray" is *hitpallel*. It is a reflexive form of the root *palal*. Elsewhere that root means to intervene, mediate or judge: Phinehas "stood up and intervened" (Psalm 106:30), and "if someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him" (1 Samuel 2:25). The first time *hitpallel* appears, God says Abraham "will pray for you" (Genesis 20:7).

Because the form is reflexive, a popular Jewish explanation says that to pray is "to judge or examine oneself". Others connect it with interceding or asking God to judge a case. **Scholars debate** the exact origin, so it is best to hold these as helpful reflections rather than certain facts.

The noun is *tefillah*, "prayer". God's house will be "a house of prayer for all peoples" (Isaiah 56:7), words Jesus quotes in the Temple (Mark 11:17). In Jewish tradition "the Tefillah" means the central prayer, the **Amidah** ("standing"), prayed standing every day.

sections.h: More words: entreat, ask, call, pour out
p: *Atar* means to entreat earnestly: "Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren" (Genesis 25:21). *Sha'al* is simply "to ask": "One thing have I asked of the LORD" (Psalm 27:4). Hannah named her son Samuel, saying, "I have asked for him from the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:20).

*Qara beshem*, "to call on the name", is the earliest description of prayer: "At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD" (Genesis 4:26). Abraham built altars and "called upon the name of the LORD" (12:8). Joel promises that "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved" (Joel 2:32), which Paul quotes in Romans 10:13.

*Siach* is an outpouring of the heart, a complaint or deep meditation. Psalm 102 is titled "A prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his *siach* before the LORD". "I pour out my complaint before him" (Psalm 142:2). Hannah too said she was "pouring out my soul before the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:15).

*Techinnah* is a plea for grace, from the root *chanan*, "to be gracious". At the Temple's dedication Solomon asks God to hear "the prayer (*tefillah*) of your servant and his plea (*techinnah*)" (1 Kings 8:28). It is the prayer of someone who has no claim except God's kindness.

*Berakhah*, "blessing", is the most typical Jewish prayer form. It begins *Barukh attah Adonai*, "Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe…" and goes on to name a gift: bread, wine, light, the Torah. Jewish tradition encourages saying many blessings each day, so that ordinary moments become moments of thanks. When Jesus "blessed" or "gave thanks" over bread (Mark 6:41; Luke 22:19), he was doing exactly this.

Deuteronomy 11:13 commands Israel to "serve him with all your heart". The Talmud asks, "What is service that is in the heart? This is prayer" (Taanit 2a). The phrase *avodah shebalev*, "service of the heart", became a classic Jewish description of prayer. After the Temple fell, prayer was understood as taking the place of the Temple service.

Because of this, the rabbis stressed *kavanah*, "focused intention" or direction of the heart. The Mishnah says the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, in order to direct their hearts to God (Mishnah Berakhot 5:1). It also warns that if someone makes his prayer a fixed routine, it is not a true plea for mercy (Mishnah Berakhot 4:4).
> Jewish prayer holds two things together: **keva**, fixed times and words, and **kavanah**, the heart truly present. One gives shape, the other gives life.

David prays "evening and morning and at noon" (Psalm 55:17). Daniel kneels "three times a day" toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). Jewish tradition teaches that Abraham set the morning prayer, Isaac the afternoon prayer (he went out to "meditate" in the field, Genesis 24:63) and Jacob the evening prayer (Talmud Berakhot 26b). Twice a day Jews also recite the **Shema**, "when you lie down and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:4–7).

The apostles kept these rhythms. Peter and John went up to the Temple "at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour" (Acts 3:1). Peter prayed at the sixth hour (Acts 10:9), and Cornelius at the ninth (10:30). The early Christian handbook called the Didache tells believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day (Didache 8:3).

The general Greek word is *proseuchomai*, "to pray", with the noun *proseuchē*, "prayer". It can even mean a **place of prayer**: in Philippi, Paul went to the riverside "where we supposed there was a place of prayer" (Acts 16:13), a Jewish meeting place. Jewish Greek writers sometimes used the word for a synagogue.

*Deomai* and *deēsis* mean petition born of need: "in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Philippians 4:6). *Aiteō* means to ask: "Ask, and it will be given to you" (Matthew 7:7). *Entynchanō* and *enteuxis* mean to intercede, to approach someone on another's behalf: the Spirit "intercedes for the saints" (Romans 8:26–27), and Paul urges "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings" for all people (1 Timothy 2:1). *Eucharisteō* means to give thanks: "give thanks in all circumstances" (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

sections.h: The Lord's Prayer in its Jewish setting
p: Jesus taught his disciples to pray, "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:9–10). Jews already called on God as "Our Father, our King" (*Avinu Malkenu*). The ancient **Kaddish** prayer begins, "Magnified and sanctified be His great name in the world He created by His will. May He establish His kingdom in your lifetime…"

The daily Amidah asks, "Forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned." Like these prayers, the Lord's Prayer is **communal**: "our", "us", "we". Even when you pray it alone, you pray as part of God's people. Jesus also warned against praying to be seen, or heaping up empty phrases (Matthew 6:5–7), the same concern as the rabbis' warnings about prayer without *kavanah*.

On the cross Jesus prayed the Psalms: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1; Mark 15:34) and "Into your hands I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:5; Luke 23:46). That second line is still sung in the Jewish hymn *Adon Olam*: "Into His hand I commit my spirit."

Hebrew has many words for prayer, and English has one favourite: "pray". *Hitpallel*, *atar*, *sha'al*, *siach* and *techinnah* are often all rendered "pray", "entreat" or "supplicate", and modern versions add "plead" or "cry for mercy". Translators do this because English readers need a familiar word, and because the exact shades of some Hebrew words are uncertain. The cost is that the variety disappears: intervening for others, pleading, simply asking, pouring out the heart and begging for grace all collapse into one grey word.

Blessing is another case. In Mark 6:41 the KJV says Jesus "blessed, and brake the loaves", and many readers picture Jesus making the bread holy. In Jewish practice the blessing is said to God: "Blessed are You… who brings forth bread from the earth." That is why the NIV gives "gave thanks". The Gospels themselves use two verbs, *eulogeō* (bless) and *eucharisteō* (give thanks), at the Last Supper (Mark 14:22–23). Both describe the same Jewish table-blessing, but English readers may think they are two different acts.

Even the English word has moved. "Pray" comes through French from the Latin *precari*, "to ask, to beg", and in older English it was used between people: "I pray thee". Over time it became a religious word only, and narrowed towards asking. The Hebrew and Greek words are wider: praise, blessing, thanks, lament and silent attention all count as prayer.

In Jesus' Judea, the rhythm of prayer followed the Temple. Lambs were offered every morning and afternoon (Exodus 29:38–42), and incense was burned with them. Luke says "the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense" (Luke 1:10). Jews far from Jerusalem prayed facing the city, as Solomon had asked and Daniel did (1 Kings 8:48; Daniel 6:10). People often prayed standing, with hands lifted (1 Kings 8:22; 1 Timothy 2:8).

Prayer also filled the home and the street. Men wore the Shema in small boxes on arm and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:8; Jesus mentions these "phylacteries" in Matthew 23:5) and fringes on their garments (Numbers 15:38–39). Meals began and ended with blessings. In the diaspora, Jews met in a *proseuchē*, a house of prayer, which Greek and Roman writers noticed as a feature of Jewish communities.

The Greco-Roman world prayed differently. Romans especially believed that a prayer had to use the exact words and name the right god, or it might fail. Many prayers were a kind of bargain, often summed up in the Latin phrase *do ut des*, "I give so that you may give". Against this background Jesus says, "do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words… your Father knows what you need" (Matthew 6:7–8). Jewish and Christian prayer was addressed to a Father, not a bargaining partner.

A common Western habit is to treat prayer as mainly private requests in spontaneous words, and to see fixed prayer as dead ritual. The Jewish lens shows a fuller picture: praise and blessing come first; asking has its place; times and shared words give shape; and the heart must be present.

Try a simple rhythm: a short prayer morning, afternoon and evening; a blessing before food and after good news; the Lord's Prayer said slowly, meaning each line; and space to pour out your heart honestly, as Hannah and the psalmists did. Prayer then becomes what the rabbis called it: the service of the heart, offered every day.

words.note: Reflexive form of palal (intervene, judge); its exact sense is debated.
words.missed: "Pray" is accurate, but it hides the root idea of stepping in, mediating or bringing a case for judgement.
words.culture: Prayer in Israel was often intercession: a prophet, priest or king standing before God for others, as Abraham, Moses and Samuel did.

words.note: In Jewish tradition "the Tefillah" is the Amidah, the standing prayer.
words.missed: "Prayer" sounds like any spoken request; in Jewish usage "the Tefillah" is a named, shared prayer said standing.
words.culture: The Amidah is prayed facing Jerusalem, feet together, softly enough that only you hear, as Hannah prayed with moving lips (1 Samuel 1:13).

words.note: Isaac pleads with God for his barren wife.
words.missed: "Entreat" or "pray" loses the strong, repeated pleading in the word.
words.culture: Childlessness brought deep grief and shame in a family culture, which is why Isaac and Hannah plead so hard.

words.note: Simple asking; Hannah "asked" God for Samuel.
words.missed: English splits sha'al into "ask", "inquire" and "borrow", so its ordinary, everyday feel is hidden.
words.culture: Israelites "asked" of God at the sanctuary, often through a priest or prophet, before battles and big decisions.

words.note: The earliest phrase for worship and prayer in the Bible.
words.missed: "Call upon" sounds like a phone call; to call on a name meant to invoke someone publicly as your lord and protector.
words.culture: Altars and calling on the name marked out land and loyalty in a world where every people called on its own gods.

words.note: Pouring out the heart honestly before God.
words.missed: The KJV's "complaint" sounds like grumbling; siach is honest outpouring, musing or meditation.
words.culture: The Psalms show that pouring out grief and protest before God was a normal part of worship, not a failure of faith.

words.note: From chanan, "be gracious": asking on the basis of God's kindness alone.
words.missed: "Supplication" is a rare English word; the Hebrew stresses asking for grace you have not earned.
words.culture: A subject asked a king for favour knowing he had no claim; that court picture lies behind techinnah.

words.note: "Blessed are You, LORD our God…": thanking God for each gift.
words.missed: English readers think "blessing" means God blesses us; a berakhah is mainly us blessing, that is praising, God.
words.culture: Jewish homes say blessings over bread, wine, light and many daily events, turning ordinary moments into thanks.

words.note: The classic rabbinic description of prayer.
words.missed: The phrase is not in English Bibles, so readers miss the link between prayer and Temple worship.
words.culture: After the Temple fell in AD 70, synagogue prayer took the place of the daily offerings in Jewish life.

words.note: Directing the heart to God while praying.
words.missed: English has no single word for it; "concentration" is too cold and "sincerity" too vague.
words.culture: The early pious ones waited quietly before praying to direct their hearts to God (Mishnah Berakhot 5:1).

words.note: The general New Testament word for praying.
words.missed: "Pray" in English once also meant simply "ask" ("I pray thee"); in Greek it is a word for prayer to God only.
words.culture: Greeks and Romans prayed to many gods with exact formulas; Jews and Christians used the same verb for the one God.

words.note: Can also mean a Jewish place of prayer.
words.missed: The KJV reads Acts 16:13 as "where prayer was wont to be made"; the word can also mean a building or place.
words.culture: In the Jewish diaspora a proseuchē was a prayer-house, sometimes by water for washing, as at Philippi.

words.note: Asking out of real need.
words.missed: "Supplication" sounds formal; deēsis is the cry of someone in real need.
words.culture: Beggars and petitioners in the Greco-Roman world made a deēsis to officials and patrons; we bring ours to God.

words.note: "Ask, and it will be given to you."
words.missed: "Ask" is right; what is lost is the bold, childlike confidence of the request in Jesus' saying.
words.culture: Jesus pictures a child asking a father for bread and fish (Matthew 7:9–11), the food of a Galilean home.

words.note: Approaching God on behalf of others.
words.missed: "Intercession" sounds churchy; in Greek it was the plain word for approaching an official on someone's behalf.
words.culture: People presented written petitions (enteuxeis) to rulers; Paul uses the word for praying "for kings and all in authority".

words.note: Thanksgiving, like the Jewish blessing over bread.
words.missed: Bibles alternate "gave thanks" and "blessed" at meals, hiding that both reflect the one Jewish table-blessing.
words.culture: From this verb comes "Eucharist", the early church's name for the Lord's Supper.

Prayer; in Jewish usage also the Amidah, the central standing prayer.
"Standing" prayer of blessings, prayed every day; also called the Tefillah.
A blessing: "Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe…"
"Service of the heart": the rabbinic name for prayer (Taanit 2a).
Focused intention: the heart directed to God in prayer.
An ancient Jewish prayer praising God's name and asking for His kingdom to come.
Greek for prayer, and also a place of prayer (Acts 16:13).
